proposedTopics.title: AVSs & operators (EigenLayer)
proposedTopics.description: EigenLayer lets restakers extend Ethereum's economic security to new services. An AVS (Autonomous Verifiable Service) is a service that uses EigenLayer operator sets. Operators run the service's off-chain software; restakers delegate stake to an operator, and operators allocate slashable magnitude to operator sets. The AVS defines tasks, evidence, and enforcement.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/avs.md define, for a toy AVS (say, a signed-price oracle), what the operators do off-chain, what a task looks like, and which misbehavior is slashable. Done when: you can name the three parties (restaker, operator, AVS) and state what the AVS must specify for slashing to be meaningful.

requirements.purpose: Model current task execution, operator roles, and AVS-owned validation and enforcement boundaries

proposedTopics.title: Restaking delegation & the security model
proposedTopics.description: Restakers deposit supported assets into EigenLayer strategies and delegate to one operator. For each strategy, an operator can split slashable magnitude across multiple operator sets, but total encumbered magnitude cannot exceed current max magnitude. This allocates one delegated pool across services without letting AVS allocations overcommit it. A slash reduces delegated stake and max magnitude, shrinking future security capacity.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/restaking-risk.md work a numeric example with 100 delegated shares, a 100% current max magnitude, allocations across three operator sets whose sum does not exceed that max, and a proportional slash in one set; recompute lost shares, max magnitude, encumbered magnitude, and free capacity. Done when: you distinguish delegation from allocation, enforce the no-overcommit invariant, and explain why a slash reduces future security capacity.

requirements.purpose: Distinguish restaker-to-operator delegation from operator-set allocation and recompute capacity after slashing

proposedTopics.title: EigenLayer slashing
proposedTopics.description: Slashing makes allocated restaked security enforceable. An operator allocates magnitude to an AVS operator set; that set's configured slasher can reduce a bounded proportion of the operator's allocation, which proportionally reduces delegated stake. EigenLayer enforces authorization and allocation bounds, but the AVS remains responsible for safe evidence and slashing policy. Core v1.13 adds a mandatory resolution delay before burnable or redistributable shares from a recorded slash can be cleared.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/eigen-slashing.md trace operator-set creation, slasher authority, allocation, a numeric slash from allocated magnitude to lost delegated shares, and the v1.13 resolution-delay boundary before clearing. Done when: you can state which address may slash, what bounds the amount, why recording and clearing a slash are distinct, and why an AVS still needs objective evidence, conservative policy, and reviewed slasher code.

proposedTopics.title: SNARKs vs STARKs
proposedTopics.description: SNARK and STARK name families, not one fixed performance profile. Common pairing-based SNARKs offer small proofs and cheap on-chain verification but may require a circuit-specific or universal setup and are not post-quantum. STARKs use transparent public randomness and hash-based assumptions, usually trading for larger proofs. Succinctness and zero-knowledge are independent properties.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/snark-vs-stark.md tabulate SNARK vs STARK on proof size, verifier cost, trusted setup, and quantum resistance. Done when: you can state which property (succinctness vs zero-knowledge) a given use case actually needs and why a trusted-setup ceremony's soundness matters for a SNARK.

requirements.purpose: Compare proof families without treating every SNARK or STARK implementation as having one fixed setup or cost profile

proposedTopics.title: Arithmetic circuits & constraint systems
proposedTopics.description: A ZK DSL compiles constrained computation into a backend intermediate representation over field elements. R1CS and PLONKish systems encode arithmetic relations differently; a witness assigns values needed to satisfy them. Unconstrained code can compute hints, but soundness requires constrained code to check every fact the proof claims.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/circuits.md express 'I know x such that x^3 + x + 5 == 35' with intermediate witnesses and explicit constraints, then show a deliberately unconstrained hint and the constraint that makes it safe. Done when: you identify public inputs, private witness values, field wraparound, and why an unchecked hint proves nothing.

requirements.purpose: Translate arithmetic into field constraints and keep witness-generation hints separate from soundness checks

proposedTopics.title: Arbitrum Nitro & interactive fraud proofs
proposedTopics.description: Nitro can replay its state-transition logic in a deterministic Wasm proving environment. Arbitrum's current BoLD dispute protocol organizes competing assertions and narrows a disputed execution history until a one-step proof resolves a single machine step on L1. One honest active validator is required during the challenge period; BoLD bounds delay under many adversarial claims.

proposedTopics.title: Sequencer, batcher & data availability
proposedTopics.description: In an OP Stack rollup, the sequencer creates L2 blocks, the batcher publishes compressed channel frames to the configured data-availability provider (Ethereum calldata or blobs for a rollup), and verifiers derive the canonical L2 chain from L1. State proposals and fault proofs are a separate commitment path. A validium keeps transaction data off Ethereum and therefore adds an external availability assumption.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is an AVS, and who are the three parties in EigenLayer?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: An AVS (Autonomous Verifiable Service) uses EigenLayer operator sets to make verifiable commitments; operators run its software backed by stake that restakers delegate and operators allocate. Pitfall: slashing is only meaningful if the AVS specifies an objectively attributable fault condition — otherwise stake can be destroyed subjectively.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is the core tradeoff of restaking the same stake across many AVSs?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Restakers delegate shares to one operator; for each strategy, that operator splits magnitude across operator sets, and total encumbered magnitude cannot exceed current max magnitude. A slash reduces the targeted allocation, delegated shares, and max magnitude, leaving less future capacity. Pitfall: delegation and allocation are separate, and operator-set allocations cannot each reuse the same 100%.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does EigenLayer's slashing framework require to protect honest restakers?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: An operator allocates a bounded magnitude to an operator set, and only that set's configured slasher may slash it; the slash proportionally reduces delegated stake. Core v1.13 delays clearing burnable or redistributable shares after the slash is recorded. EigenLayer enforces authority and allocation bounds, not the correctness of an AVS's evidence. Pitfall: unsafe slasher code or subjective evidence can still destroy honestly delegated stake.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What distinguishes cryptographic from crypto-economic verifiability for an EigenCloud service?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Cryptographic verifiability supplies a proof; reproducible execution lets another party recompute; crypto-economic accountability penalizes attributable faults. Pitfall: a product label does not tell you which guarantee applies—identify verifier, evidence, failure model, and any stake actually at risk.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is a tokenized Treasury only as safe as its off-chain wrapper?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The token represents a legally defined claim on an off-chain portfolio or note; code cannot itself establish legal title, custody, valuation, eligibility, or redemption. Trust rests on the product's issuer/fund, service providers, custody and transfer infrastructure. Pitfall: BUIDL, OUSG, USDY, and rUSDY have different assets and yield mechanics.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What must a compliant RWA token add over a plain ERC-20, and what does it break?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: ERC-3643 separates identity-registry eligibility from global compliance and adds pre-checks, pause/freeze, recovery, and agent-authorized lifecycle actions such as forced transfer. Pitfall: integrations that assume every address can receive and transfer a plain ERC-20 may revert or become unusable.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why do RWAs need proof-of-reserve oracles, and what's the residual trust?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A PoR feed attests a defined reserve quantity; a consumer can compare normalized reserves with liabilities only after checking units, decimals, sign, and freshness. Pitfall: the feed does not independently prove legal title, redemption rights, NAV, or that its attested asset matches the token liability.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Contrast SNARKs and STARKs on setup, proof size, and quantum resistance.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Common pairing-based SNARKs offer small proofs and cheap verification but may use circuit-specific or universal setup and are not post-quantum; STARKs use transparent public randomness and hash assumptions, usually with larger proofs. Pitfall: these are families—state the concrete system before claiming setup, size, or verifier cost.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What do ZK systems actually prove, and what is the witness?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A backend proves satisfaction of its compiled field constraints using witness assignments. R1CS and PLONKish systems encode relations differently; DSL branches/loops are compiled or bounded. Pitfall: unconstrained hints add no soundness unless constrained code checks their claimed result, and Field arithmetic wraps modulo the backend field.

proposedPrompts.promptText: In a Noir `main`, what distinguishes public from private inputs, and how do you verify?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Inputs marked `pub` are public; unmarked inputs are private witness; `assert` adds constraints. Current Nargo compiles/executes (`nargo execute`) and a backend such as Barretenberg proves/verifies (`bb prove`, `bb verify`). Pitfall: pin compatible versions and remember public values are revealed with the proof.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write and prove a Noir circuit for a hash preimage, then verify it.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Write a valid Noir hash constraint with x private and the digest public; `nargo execute` emits circuit+witness, then `bb prove` and `bb verify`. A wrong preimage must fail execution/proving. Pin Nargo, bb, and the selected hash/proof mode.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does an on-chain SNARK verifier work, and where is its trust anchored?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A generated verifier checks backend-specific proof bytes and public inputs against a verification key tied to one circuit and proving configuration. Pitfall: mismatched circuit, key, backend version, hash mode, serialization, or public-input order invalidates the boundary; not every SNARK verifier uses pairings.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Across ZK rollups, privacy apps, and identity proofs, what is the common pattern?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Prove a fact while hiding the witness: rollups prove correct L2 execution to L1 (validity), privacy apps prove a statement without revealing inputs, identity proofs reveal a predicate (over 18, is human) not the data. Pitfall: define public inputs vs private witness precisely — a value accidentally made public defeats the privacy goal.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a Nitro interactive fraud proof keep L1 cost low?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Nitro supplies deterministic Wasm execution; BoLD organizes competing assertions and narrows the disputed history until L1 verifies a one-step proof. Pitfall: one honest validator must actively participate within the challenge period; BoLD bounds delay from many adversarial claims rather than removing that liveness assumption.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What are the two halves of the OP Stack fault-proof system?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The deterministic fault-proof program derives L2 output from agreed inputs; Cannon is an FPVM that generates a trace off-chain and verifies one instruction on-chain, while the dispute game narrows claims. Pitfall: op-program is transitioning to kona-client, so pin the game type and implementation version.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is data availability, not the state root, the security linchpin of a rollup?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The sequencer creates blocks; the batcher publishes compressed channel frames to Ethereum calldata or blobs; verifiers derive the canonical L2 chain from L1 data. A state root alone cannot reconstruct execution. Pitfall: a validium uses external DA, adding an availability assumption rather than merely 'posting only a root.'
